name: Baptist movement
notes: Origins traced to English dissenters; first Baptist church in Amsterdam in 1609.
summary: A worldwide family of churches that joins personal faith and baptism to the idea of a voluntarily gathered congregation.
formation_narrative: English dissenters sought churches whose membership rested on professed faith rather than residence in a parish. Smyth and Helwys established an early Baptist congregation in Amsterdam around 1609; Helwys returned to England around 1612. Later Particular Baptists developed another influential English stream. General and Particular Baptists differed over salvation and election, and subsequent migration, missions, revival, and Black church organization produced many separate conventions. Baptist identity therefore describes a family, not one governing institution.
core_beliefs: Believer’s baptism: baptism follows a person’s own confession of faith rather than being conferred simply because the person was born into a Christian household. Immersion became widespread, but the Amsterdam beginnings should not be read as already having every later practice.

Gathered churches: a congregation is a community of people who intentionally covenant together. Local autonomy means a convention ordinarily cannot govern a congregation as a bishop or presbytery would.

Scripture and conscience: Baptists appeal to the Bible as their norm and have made influential arguments for religious liberty. They nevertheless disagree about predestination, ministry, biblical interpretation, and participation in wider church bodies.

profile_scope: The 1609 date is a conventional early-church milestone, not evidence that every Baptist body descends institutionally from this congregation.
ending_narrative: The Baptist family continues through many autonomous churches and conventions. The graph’s later conventions are branches and partners, not a collective replacement for a terminated parent.

name: Triennial Convention
notes: 1814 missionary convention; reorganization/name transition to American Baptist Missionary Union in 1846, with later continuity in International Ministries. Distinct from the Northern Baptist Convention founded in 1907.
summary: An early national Baptist foreign-missions convention, not a denomination exercising authority over local churches.
formation_narrative: Baptist support for overseas missions produced the General Missionary Convention in 1814, popularly called Triennial because of its meeting cycle. Mission societies coordinated work that individual autonomous congregations could not easily sustain alone. Conflict over appointing slaveholders as missionaries contributed to Southern Baptist organization in 1845. Northern mission societies later participated in the coordination established by the Northern Baptist Convention in 1907; that is a broader institutional history than a simple renaming of this convention.
core_beliefs: Missionary cooperation: churches pooled resources to send and support missionaries without surrendering congregational government.
Baptist church membership: participating churches shared a believer-church heritage, but this convention’s defining purpose was foreign missions rather than a new complete doctrinal system.
Limits of cooperation: slavery exposed deep moral and sectional divisions inside a network that otherwise claimed a common mission.

name: Southern Baptist Convention
notes: Separated from the Triennial Convention in 1845.
summary: A cooperative convention of autonomous Baptist churches, established in the slaveholding South in 1845.
formation_narrative: Southern organizers created a separate missionary convention after national mission agencies would not accept slaveholding missionary candidates. The convention developed common mission, educational, and publishing institutions while affirming local church autonomy. Its contemporary statement of faith defines a conservative evangelical identity. In 1995 the convention formally acknowledged slavery’s part in its origins and repented of racism; its founding context and subsequent self-examination both belong in the account.
core_beliefs: Biblical authority: the Baptist Faith and Message describes Scripture as wholly trustworthy and the standard for teaching and conduct.
Salvation and church membership: repentance and faith in Christ precede believer’s baptism by immersion; the local congregation governs its own life.

Cooperation with boundaries: churches voluntarily cooperate in missions while doctrinal standards shape convention institutions. The confession also teaches a male pastoral office; this is a Southern Baptist position, not a rule for all Baptists.

name: American Baptist Churches USA
notes: Reorganization of the Triennial Convention in 1907.
summary: A Baptist communion combining autonomous congregations, cooperative mission, and considerable theological and cultural diversity.
formation_narrative: Northern Baptist churches coordinated mission societies through a convention organized in 1907. It became the American Baptist Convention in 1950 and American Baptist Churches USA in 1972. The present body maintains a connection to earlier missionary work without being simply the Triennial Convention under a new name. Its history includes both evangelistic mission and social service, with unity negotiated among churches that do not agree on every question.
core_beliefs: Christ-centered faith: confession of Christ’s saving work accompanies an emphasis on the believer’s direct relationship with God.
Local freedom and responsibility: congregations govern themselves, practice believer’s baptism, and cooperate in wider mission.
Religious liberty and diversity: freedom of worship and opinion is valued within a shared Christian witness; one faction’s conclusions should not be assigned to every church.

name: National Baptist Convention, USA
notes: Formed in 1895 by merger of multiple Baptist conventions.
summary: A historically Black Baptist convention created to coordinate mission, education, and the work of autonomous churches.
formation_narrative: In 1895 earlier Black Baptist conventions united their mission and educational efforts. This organization grew in a society shaped by slavery’s aftermath and racial exclusion, creating institutions under Black leadership. Later disputes over the publishing board and over leadership and civil-rights strategy produced separate conventions. Organizational separation should not be mistaken for an entirely new theology each time.
core_beliefs: Baptist Christian faith: the convention’s Articles of Faith use the New Hampshire confessional tradition to express beliefs about Scripture, salvation, and the church.
Autonomous churches: cooperation in mission and education operates through a convention rather than a hierarchy controlling every congregation.
Institution-building: publishing, training, and missionary work express a corporate religious vocation as well as the pursuit of Black institutional independence.

name: National Baptist Convention of America International
summary: A historically Black Baptist convention emerging from the 1915 conflict over control of Baptist publishing.
formation_narrative: The National Baptist publishing-board controversy divided leaders who otherwise shared much Baptist theology. The National Baptist Convention of America developed as a separate cooperative body rather than as the result of a new doctrine of baptism or salvation. Its history is therefore best explained through institutional authority, publishing, and autonomous Black church cooperation, with attention to subsequent organizational changes that need further detailed research.
core_beliefs: Shared Baptist inheritance: local congregations emphasize the Bible, conversion, and believer’s baptism, but practice varies among autonomous churches.
Cooperative autonomy: the convention coordinates ministries while the congregation remains the basic governing church body.
Confessional caution: the historical survey used here reports no single convention-wide statement of faith; it would be misleading to assign the SBC confession to this body.

name: Progressive National Baptist Convention
summary: A historically Black Baptist convention whose formation joined church-governance disputes to support for civil-rights activism.
formation_narrative: The 1961 National Baptist Convention meeting exposed conflict over incumbent leadership and the use of nonviolent direct action. Ministers associated with Gardner Taylor and supporters of Martin Luther King Jr.’s approach formed a separate convention in Cincinnati that November. Its distinctive historical role is the institutional space it provided for civil-rights advocacy within a Baptist framework, rather than a wholly separate baptismal theology.
core_beliefs: Baptist church life: congregations retain a shared believer-church heritage and local independence.
Faith and public action: Christian witness is connected with racial justice and nonviolent efforts to change discriminatory institutions.
Freedom within fellowship: the convention’s cooperative identity should not be reduced to a single compulsory creed or one political personality.

name: Venture Church Network
notes: Formerly Conservative Baptist Association of America; formed in 1947 after separation from the Northern Baptist Convention.
summary: An evangelical Baptist network continuing the Conservative Baptist Association’s emphasis on doctrinal conviction and voluntary cooperation.
formation_narrative: Conservative Baptists first established mission agencies and then, in 1947, a separate association of churches amid conflict over theological direction in northern Baptist institutions. The present Venture Church Network describes that separation as a defense of historic evangelical convictions. Its network structure aims to strengthen local churches without replacing their government; the account of the dispute is the organization’s own interpretation and should be read as such.
core_beliefs: Biblical authority: its statement teaches that Scripture is inspired, trustworthy, and sufficient for faith and conduct.
Evangelical salvation: the network centers its message on Christ and the gospel rather than treating social or institutional cooperation as sufficient in itself.
Local churches in partnership: shared doctrine supports mission and leadership development while churches retain their own life and governance.
